stem: An 8-year-old boy with asthma has monthly attacks over winter, was discharged from PICU a few days ago after a severe attack, has been off oxygen since yesterday, wakes at night at least 5 days each week, wheezes with exercise, and uses ventolin at least once daily. When not well, what preventer and dose would you prescribe?

options.text: Flixotide junior (50mcg) 2 puffs BD
Flixotide junior (50mcg) 2 puffs twice per day
Seretide 125 mcg 1 puff BD
Seretide 125 mcg 1 puff twice per day
Seretide 250 mcg 1 puff BD
Seretide 250 mcg 1 puff twice per day
Flixotide junior (50mcg) 4 puffs BD
Flixotide junior (50mcg) 4 puffs twice per day

explanation: This child has very poorly controlled, severe asthma with frequent nocturnal symptoms, exercise symptoms, frequent reliever use, and a recent PICU admission. A high-dose inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting beta-agonist preventer is appropriate among the options provided. Seretide 250 mcg 1 puff twice daily is the highest preventer option listed.
rationale: The source item asks for a preventer choice in a child with severe persistent, poorly controlled asthma. Among the existing options, the strongest ICS/LABA regimen is the best single answer.

optionExplanations.A: Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid only; insufficient for this level of poor control.
optionExplanations.B: Same as A; still low-dose inhaled corticosteroid only.
optionExplanations.C: ICS/LABA, but lower than the best option listed for this severe presentation.
optionExplanations.D: Same medication strength as C; wording only differs.
optionExplanations.E: Higher than 125 mcg but still below the highest listed preventer dose.
optionExplanations.F: Highest-dose preventer option provided; best fit for severe uncontrolled asthma in this item.
optionExplanations.G: Higher-dose ICS, but still without LABA and likely inadequate for this severity.
optionExplanations.H: Same as G; wording only differs.
